paragraphs: Decision center: the work of drilling and boring machine tool setters, operators, and tenders is to turn these front-end conditions — drawings, work orders, and process requirements, workpiece material, dimensions, and tolerances, and machine tools, cutting tools, measuring tools, and fixtures — into a qualified part that can be drilled, bored, reamed, milled, and countersunk, that can be measured and checked, and that holds tolerances and safety boundaries: first read the machining instructions, work orders, and drawings to determine dimensions, surfaces, operations, fixturing, and tool requirements, then establish a zero reference point and lay out lines, then select and set cutting speed, feed, depth of cut, and tools according to the material and requirements and install the tools, then position and clamp the workpiece, operate the machine to engage the automatic feed to complete drilling, boring, reaming, milling, and countersinking with coolant or cutting oil, then verify dimensions and tolerances with calipers and micrometers or gauges, and finally replace and sharpen tools, carry out equipment and tooling maintenance, and record and report anomalies. The point of judgment is not 'can a hole be drilled' but whether every step of the chain — reading drawings, laying out, fixturing, machining, measuring, and tool changing and maintenance — is accurate, verifiable, and handled according to the drawings and safety procedures.

Suitable for a first try: willing to stand for long periods in a machining workshop and work machine tools and measuring tools by hand; able to work according to drawings, tolerances, and process requirements and stay focused and patient; able to withstand noise and cutting fluid, coolant, oil mist, and metal chips and wear protective equipment; willing to do dimensional measurement, self-inspection, equipment maintenance, and record keeping and to accept shift work and piece-rate or quota rhythms.

Needs caution: if you expect this job to be in an office or to require only pressing a button without reading drawings, or you are unwilling to wear protective equipment and follow machine tool safety guards and chip, oil mist, and measuring tool calibration requirements (starting the machine without clamping, cleaning chips directly with your hands, skipping self-inspection, or changing parameters at will beyond the process range), or you find it hard to maintain attention on dimensions and tolerances for long periods in repetitive drilling and boring operations, then the actual work experience usually does not match the expectation.

Low-risk verification: using the fictional drawings, work orders, process cards, and measuring tool readings provided on this page, complete a paper exercise that 'arranges the drilling and boring sequence according to the drawings and work orders — writes out tool selection, fixturing, and alignment notes according to the cutting parameters — and fills in one dimensional measurement, self-inspection, and equipment and tool inspection record', only to verify whether you are willing to check item by item according to the drawings, tolerances, and process and to record truthfully. The exercise uses fictional materials and does not involve real machine tools, cutting tools, or workpieces, and it does not constitute a quality system, process, or safety compliance conclusion, nor is it equivalent to job training, a skill level, or machine tool operation authorization.

Decision center: whether drawings, tolerances, and process requirements can be turned into a chain of machining and self-inspection records that the team, inspection, and the next operation can all take up and verify.

The work is mainly in machining workshop positions with frequent communication with the team: teamwork 'extremely important' 56% (another 23% very important), face-to-face discussions every day 52% (another 41% weekly or more), continuous contact with others 51% (another 26% most of the time), telephone conversations every day 21% (another 44% never), email use every day 35% (another 42% never); decision freedom 'very large' 40% (another 40% some), precision or accuracy 'extremely important' 70% (another 30% very important), time pressure every day 51%; work hours 'regular' 80% (another 20% irregular); standing continuously 25% (another 50% more than half), using hands continuously 57% (another 33% more than half); exposure to hazardous equipment every day 54%, exposure to contaminants every day 61%, wearing common protective or safety equipment every day 93%, exposure to noise every day 56% (another 31% weekly or more), exposure to extreme heat or extreme cold 'weekly or more' 29%; pace determined by equipment speed 'extremely important' 52%, automation level 'moderately automated' 43%; repeating the same tasks 'extremely important' 26%; consequences of error 'extremely serious' 29% (another 27% very serious, 26% serious); working more than 40 hours per week 79%. The workplace is a machining workshop and machine tool operating position, and the pace is determined by the operation cycle, equipment speed, batch, and delivery date.

Similar names do not mean the same duties: this page is O*NET-SOC 51-4032.00 Drilling and Boring Machine Tool Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic. Adjacent positions have different duties — lathe operators operate lathes to cut rotating workpiece surfaces; metal milling and planing machine tool operators operate milling machines and planers for milling and planing of flat surfaces, grooves, and steps; grinding machine operators operate grinders for grinding and polishing; extruding, drawing, forging, and rolling machine setters and operators operate forming equipment to complete extrusion, drawing, forging, and rolling; industrial machinery mechanics handle equipment installation and repair; welders, cutters, and brazers handle welding, cutting, and brazing; earth drillers and oil and gas rotary drill operators work on surface and oil and gas well drilling. This occupation is set on setting up and operating or tending drilling machines and boring machines to drill, bore, ream, mill, and countersink metal or plastic workpieces. Process and quality system or safety and occupational health requirements are governed by the regulations and standards of the relevant jurisdiction and by plant systems, are not inferred from the job title, and must not exceed authorization to issue inspection-pass, process, or safety and compliance conclusions externally.

Inputs that must be verified: machining instructions and work orders and drawings and process cards (dimensions, tolerances, surface requirements, operations, fixturing, and tool requirements), workpiece material and blank and heat treatment state, the model and condition of machine tools and spindles and cutting tools and fixtures and measuring tools and tooling, cutting speed and feed and depth of cut and cooling method parameters, the zero reference point and layout basis, and measuring tool calibration status and inspection and self-inspection requirements. Things that must not be done: machining without reading drawings or from experience, omitting alignment and clamping and self-inspection, using uncalibrated measuring tools to judge acceptance, changing cutting parameters or tools at will beyond the process range, working with defective machine tools or missing safety guards, cleaning chips directly with your hands or operating beyond protective devices, and concealing or delaying the reporting of dimensional out-of-tolerance, equipment anomalies, or personal injury.

The fit judgment should be made by combining whether you can stand for long periods in a machining workshop and operate machine tools by hand, whether you can work according to drawings, tolerances, and process requirements and stay focused and patient, whether you can withstand noise and cutting fluid, oil mist, and metal chip environments, whether you can do dimensional measurement, self-inspection, equipment maintenance, and record keeping, and whether you are clear about your duties, authorization, and quality and safety boundaries; it is not replaced by a self-assessment of being 'strong' or 'handy'; all of this must be confirmed in supervised actual machining and team observation.

All exercises on this page use fictional materials; real machine tool operation and process, quality, work safety, and occupational health must be undertaken by organizations and personnel with the corresponding position training that follow the regulations and standards of the relevant jurisdiction and plant systems; individuals must not exceed authorization to issue inspection-pass, process, safety, or compliance conclusions externally, and this page does not constitute process, quality, safety, occupational health, or legal advice.

The work object of this occupation is drilling and boring tasks in a machining workshop: machining instructions and work orders and drawings and process cards (dimensions, tolerances, surface requirements, operations, fixturing, and tool requirements), metal or plastic workpieces and blanks and semi-finished products, drilling machines and boring machines (including single-spindle and multi-spindle drilling machines) and spindles and cutting tools and fixtures and tooling and measuring tools, parameters such as cutting speed and feed and depth of cut and cooling method, and dimensional measurement, self-inspection, and equipment and tool inspection records. The output is machining results and records that meet the drawings and tolerances: drilled, bored, reamed, milled, and countersunk work completed by operation, dimensions, tolerances, and surfaces checked against the drawings, and verifiable measurement, self-inspection, tool change and maintenance, and anomaly reporting records. The basis for judgment is the drawings, work orders, process, tolerances, measuring tool readings, and machine tool safety guard requirements, not personal habits or the job title.

Judgment one: whether the drawings, work orders, and process requirements are read clearly — checking against dimensions, tolerances, surfaces, operations, fixturing, and tool requirements rather than starting the machine from experience.

Judgment two: whether fixturing, alignment, and the zero reference point are in place — positioning and clamping the workpiece and using a dial indicator or layout to establish the zero reference point and reference lines rather than clamping casually and machining.

Judgment three: whether cutting parameters and tools are selected on a documented basis — selecting and setting cutting speed, feed, depth of cut, and tools according to the material and requirements and installing them properly rather than adjusting parameters by feel.

Judgment four: whether the machining process and cooling are controlled — operating the machine to engage the automatic feed per procedure, using coolant or cutting oil, and observing drilling or boring machine operation to find problems rather than not looking and not asking.

Judgment five: whether dimensions and tolerances are checked with measuring tools — using calipers and micrometers or gauges to verify that machined parts meet specification and handling out-of-tolerance as required rather than judging acceptance by feel.

Judgment six: whether tool changing, sharpening, maintenance, and anomalies are held — replacing and sharpening worn tools and performing equipment and tooling maintenance and reporting and handing over per the system when dimensional out-of-tolerance, equipment anomalies, or personal injury occur, rather than concealing or delaying.

The work of drilling and boring machine tool setters, operators, and tenders can be divided into three connected but independent work surfaces. The first is drawing reading and preparation: study the machining instructions and work orders and drawings to determine dimensions, tolerances, surfaces, operations, fixturing, and tool requirements, check the workpiece material and blank, establish a zero reference point and lay out reference lines and machining positions on the workpiece, select and set cutting speed, feed, depth of cut, and tools according to the material and requirements, and install the tools into the spindle. The second is fixturing and machining: position and secure the workpiece on the worktable with bolts and fixtures and clamps and shims, operate the machine controller to lower the tool and engage the automatic feed, operate single-spindle or multi-spindle drilling machines for drilling, boring, reaming, milling, and countersinking, turn valves to direct coolant or cutting oil to the cutting zone, use a dial indicator mounted on the spindle to verify that the workpiece reference line is parallel to the worktable's axis of rotation, and when necessary operate tracing attachments to reproduce contours from a template or model. The third is inspection and maintenance and records: use calipers and micrometers or fixed or telescoping gauges to verify that machined parts meet specification, replace and sharpen worn tools, do small assemblies, lift and move workpieces, maintain machine tools and tooling, and record machining, measurement, tool change, and anomaly data and report and hand over as required. All three work surfaces proceed within the drawings, process, tolerances, measuring tools, and machine tool safety guard requirements.
Drawing reading and preparation

Executable machining, fixturing, and tool key points and operation checklist, zero reference point and layout and alignment records, cutting parameter and tool selection and installation records
Fixturing and machining

Position and secure the workpiece with fixtures and clamps and shims → operate the machine to lower the tool and engage the automatic feed → operate single-spindle or multi-spindle drilling machines to complete drilling, boring, reaming, milling, and countersinking → direct coolant or cutting oil → use a dial indicator to verify that the reference line is parallel to the axis of rotation
Records of drilling, boring, reaming, milling, and countersinking completed by operation, cooling and observation and alignment records, fixturing and alignment and process adjustment records
Inspection and maintenance and records

Verify dimensions and tolerances with measuring tools and handle out-of-tolerance → replace and sharpen worn tools and do small assemblies → maintain machine tools and tooling → record machining, measurement, tool change, and anomaly data and report and hand over as required

Where are the boundaries between drilling and boring machine tool setters, operators, and tenders and lathe operators, metal milling and planing machine tool operators, grinding machine operators, extruding, drawing, forging, and rolling machine setters and operators, industrial machinery mechanics, and earth drillers?

Drilling and boring 51-4032 is distinguished from turning 51-4034, milling and planing 51-4035, grinding 51-4033, and forging 51-4022 mainly by process; oil and gas services 47-5013 is not earth drilling, and the latter 47-5023 does not include oil and gas. Actual overlapping skills must be verified against equipment and operations and cannot be mutually recognized directly from similar names.
Core purpose

Turn drawings, tolerances, and process requirements into drilling and boring results that meet specification: drawings read clearly, fixturing and alignment in place, parameters and tools selected on a documented basis, machining and cooling controlled, and dimensions and tolerances within limits.

Core purposes of adjacent positions: turning ensures rotating surface machining; milling and planing ensure flat surface, groove, and step machining; grinding ensures precision and surface quality; forming equipment ensures extrusion, drawing, forging, and rolling forming; equipment repair ensures equipment availability; drilling ensures surface and downhole hole making.
Main objects and basis

The objects are metal or plastic workpieces and blanks and semi-finished products, drilling machines and boring machines and spindles and cutting tools and fixtures and tooling and measuring tools, parameters such as cutting speed and feed and depth of cut and cooling method, and dimensional measurement, self-inspection, and equipment and tool inspection records; the basis is the drawings, work orders, process, tolerances, measuring tool readings, and machine tool safety guard requirements.

Objects and basis of adjacent positions: rotating parts and chucks and tool posts (turning process); flat plates and grooves and milling cutters and planing tools (milling and planing process); grinding wheels and the grinding process; molds and forming equipment and pressure and temperature parameters (forming process); equipment and spare parts and maintenance manuals (maintenance procedures); drilling tools and boreholes and geological conditions (drilling procedures).
Core process

Drawing reading and preparation → fixturing and alignment → drilling, boring, reaming, milling, and countersinking with cooling → verification with measuring tools and handling of out-of-tolerance → tool changing and sharpening and maintenance and records and anomaly reporting.

Processes of adjacent positions: fixturing and turning and measurement (lathe operators); fixturing and milling and planing and measurement (milling and planing); fixturing and grinding and measurement (grinding machine operators); heating or extruding or drawing or forging and forming (forming equipment); inspection and disassembly and replacement and adjustment (repair); positioning and drilling and coring and wall protection (drilling).
Main outputs

Records of drilling, boring, reaming, milling, and countersinking completed by operation, fixturing and alignment and parameter and tool records, dimensional measurement and self-inspection records, tool change and sharpening and equipment and tooling maintenance records, and anomaly reporting and handover records.

Outputs of adjacent positions: turned parts and measurement records; milled and planed parts and measurement records; ground parts and surface quality records; formed parts and pressure and temperature records; repair and adjustment and operation records; drilled holes and core samples and geological records.
Responsible parties

This occupation bears execution responsibility for setting up and operating or tending drilling and boring machine tools according to drawings and process to complete machining, self-inspection, and maintenance; process design, quality judgment, and equipment repair responsibilities are borne by the process, inspection, and equipment departments according to systems and authorization.

Responsibilities of adjacent positions: turning and milling and planing and grinding are borne by the respective machine tool operators and their organizations; forming is borne by forming equipment operators and their organizations; equipment repair is borne by mechanics and the equipment department; drilling is borne by the drilling operator and its organization.
Collaboration and supervision

Collaborate with the team leader and process, inspection, equipment repair, and upstream and downstream operations, and adjust priorities according to the operation cycle, delivery date, and batch; immediately report dimensional out-of-tolerance, equipment anomalies, personal injury, and matters beyond authorization.

Collaboration of adjacent positions: lathe operators and milling and planing and grinding interface with process and inspection; forming interfaces with molds and heat treatment and inspection; repair interfaces with production and spare parts; drilling interfaces with geology and well control and the project department.
Conclusion boundaries

Do not machine without reading drawings or from experience, do not omit alignment and clamping and self-inspection, do not use uncalibrated measuring tools to judge acceptance, do not change cutting parameters or tools at will beyond the process range, do not work with defective machine tools or missing safety guards, do not clean chips directly with your hands or operate beyond protective devices, do not conceal or delay reporting dimensional out-of-tolerance and equipment anomalies and personal injury, and do not issue inspection-pass or process or safety or compliance conclusions externally beyond authorization.

The boundaries of adjacent positions are determined by their respective process, equipment, qualification systems, and the regulations and standards of the relevant jurisdiction; similar job titles do not mean the duties are interchangeable.
In this job, which judgments are most prone to error, and how should they be verified?

Common errors cluster in four areas: first, starting the machine without reading the drawings, work orders, and process clearly, resulting in dimensions, tolerances, and operations not matching and rework; second, fixturing, alignment, and the zero reference point not being in place, resulting in offset hole positions and parallelism or perpendicularity not meeting requirements; third, improper selection of cutting parameters and tools or insufficient cooling, resulting in dimensional out-of-tolerance, unacceptable surface quality, and abnormal tool wear; fourth, uncalibrated measuring tools or omitted self-inspection and missing tool change and maintenance and anomaly reporting, resulting in batch out-of-tolerance, equipment failure, and untraceability. The verification method is that each item has a basis that can be looked back on: machining, fixturing, and tool key points and operation checklist, zero reference point and layout and alignment records, cutting parameter and tool selection and installation records, and dimensional measurement and self-inspection and tool change and maintenance and anomaly reporting records, rather than memory or verbal understanding.

Its 17 tasks are 16 Core and 1 Supplemental: checking dimensions and tolerances with gauges 96, reading instructions and work orders and drawings 93, automatic feed 89, aligning with a dial indicator 87, zeroing the reference point 87, replacing worn tools 87, selecting speed, feed, depth of cut, and tools 86, fixturing 85, observing operation 83, lifting/directing lifting 81, cooling valves 79, installing tools 79, small assemblies 73 (such as fastening nuts, bolts, and screws), single and multi-spindle drilling machines 73, laying out 73, sharpening on a grinding wheel 67. Tracing attachment contouring 45 is Supplemental and is not core for everyone. The position itself includes dimensional verification and small assemblies; mechanical maintenance is a separately listed general activity, and a 73-point assembly task cannot be treated as a maintenance task; major design/maintenance and signing authority must be verified against the actual division of work.

This table compares 'drilling and boring machine tool setters, operators, and tenders' row by row with six adjacent positions that are easily confused within the same machining content or have rotation and transfer relationships, by core work and outputs, key differences, and selection basis. The purpose of the comparison is not to rank them but to explain their respective duty boundaries and authorization scopes — in particular, process design authority, material and strength judgment authority, quality system certification authority, and equipment repair responsibility cannot be assumed by this occupation as well.

The comparison should rest on three things: first, the work object (metal or plastic workpieces and blanks, rotating parts and chucks, flat plates and grooves, grinding wheels and surfaces, molds and forming equipment, equipment and spare parts, boreholes and geology); second, the basis and authorization (the respective application of drawings and work orders and process and tolerances and measuring tool readings and machine tool safety guard requirements, turning process, milling and planing process, grinding process, forming process, maintenance procedures, and drilling procedures); third, outputs and responsibility (who is responsible for completing drilling and boring machining per the drawings and for self-inspection and maintenance, who is responsible for turning or milling and planing or grinding, who is responsible for forming, who is responsible for equipment availability, and who is responsible for hole making). When the three are inconsistent, the actual duties of the position and the process, equipment, and authorization documents prevail.

The selection basis can follow three lines: if you want to set up and operate or tend drilling machines and boring machines in a machining workshop according to drawings and process to complete drilling, boring, reaming, milling, and countersinking, this page's occupation is the closest fit; if you want to do other cutting processes such as turning or milling and planing or grinding, lathe operator or metal milling and planing machine tool operator or grinding machine operator are adjacent paths; if you want to operate forming equipment or repair equipment or weld or drill, extruding, drawing, forging, and rolling machine setters and operators or industrial machinery mechanics or welding personnel or earth drillers are another path. When transferring positions, what needs to be filled in is object knowledge and process and equipment and qualifications, not just proficiency.

paragraphs: Lathe operators (51-4034.00)

Operate lathes for cutting rotating workpiece surfaces, responsible for fixturing and tool selection and sharpening and turning internal and external cylindrical surfaces, end faces, tapered surfaces, and threads, and checking precision and error with measuring tools.

The machining motion and object differ: lathe operators rotate the workpiece while the tool feeds, mainly machining rotating surfaces; this page's occupation rotates the tool while the workpiece or spindle feeds, mainly machining holes and hole systems and flat surfaces and grooves. The process, tools, and measuring tools they rely on differ and cannot be interchanged by name.

If you want to do rotating body turning, you can choose the lathe operator direction and check the corresponding skill level requirements; if you want to do drilling and boring hole system machining, this page's occupation is the closest fit.
Metal milling and planing machine tool operators (51-4035.00)

Operate milling machines and planers to perform milling and planing of flat surfaces, grooves, steps, angles, and curved surfaces on workpieces, responsible for fixturing and machine adjustment and selection of milling cutters and planing tools and inspection.

The machine tools and machining content differ: milling and planing operations focus on flat surface, groove, and profile machining on milling machines and planers; this page's occupation focuses on hole and hole system machining on drilling machines and boring machines. The machine tools, tools, and inspection focus differ, and the tasks and outputs cannot be interchanged.

If you want to do flat surface, groove, and profile milling and planing, you can choose the metal milling and planing machine tool operator direction; if you want to do drilling, boring, and reaming, this page's occupation is more suitable.
Grinding machine operators (51-4033.00)

The object and precision target differ: grinding machine operators use grinding wheels to grind, lap, and polish workpieces to obtain high precision and low surface roughness; this page's occupation uses drilling and boring cutting to form holes and flat surfaces, with a different precision target and process basis, and the grinding operation is usually a subsequent finishing step.

If you want to do high-precision and surface quality grinding, you can choose the grinding machine operator direction; if you want to do drilling and boring cutting, this page's occupation is the closest fit.
Forging machine operators (51-4022.00)

The tasks and principle differ: forging machine operators operate forging presses to plastically form metal under heat or at room temperature and control die forging and pressure and temperature; this page's occupation removes material by cutting to form holes and flat surfaces, which is cold cutting rather than pressure forming.

If you want to do forging and pressure forming, you can choose the forging machine operator direction; if you want to do the drilling and boring steps of cutting, this page's occupation is more suitable.
Industrial machinery mechanics (49-9041.00)

Duties and authorization differ: industrial machinery mechanics are responsible for equipment installation, servicing, troubleshooting, and preventive maintenance and for determining equipment availability; this page's occupation is responsible for operating machine tools per the drawings to complete machining, self-inspection, and routine maintenance and does not bear equipment repair or availability determination duties.

If you want to do equipment repair and troubleshooting, you can take the industrial machinery mechanic path and check the corresponding training requirements; if you want to do machine tool machining operations, this page's occupation is the closest fit.
Earth drillers, oil and gas (47-5023.00)

The object and industry differ: earth drillers perform drilling, sampling, and hole making on the ground surface and in rock and soil or boreholes; this page's occupation machines holes and hole systems in mechanical parts on machine tools, and the work object, environment, and industry standards are completely different.

If you want to do surface and downhole drilling, you can choose the earth driller direction and check the drilling and safety requirements; if you want to do drilling and boring of mechanical parts, this page's occupation is more suitable.

Write a paragraph on dimensional and tolerance judgment and out-of-tolerance handling based on the measuring tool readings.

Fill in one equipment and tool inspection and dimensional measurement and self-inspection record and anomaly reporting and handover form.

Redo it under time limits and record your energy and the types of errors.

Compare the two versions of the plan and write down continue / caution / stop and the reasons.

entries: Day 1 judgment: whether uncertain items in the material were honestly marked rather than guessed and filled in.

subject.summary: Drilling and boring machine tool setters, operators, and tenders (U.S. side O*NET-SOC 51-4032.00, Drilling and Boring Machine Tool Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic) are the drilling and boring machine tool setup and operation positions in a machining workshop: they set up and operate or tend drilling machines and boring machines to drill, bore, ream, mill, and countersink metal or plastic workpieces; the work includes studying the machining instructions and work orders and drawings to determine dimensions, tolerances, operations, fixturing, and tool requirements, establishing a zero reference point and laying out lines, selecting and setting cutting speed, feed, depth of cut, and tools according to the material and requirements and installing the tools into the spindle, positioning and securing the workpiece with fixtures and clamps, operating the machine controller to lower the tool and engage the automatic feed, using a dial indicator mounted on the spindle to verify that the reference line is parallel to the worktable's axis of rotation, turning valves to direct coolant or cutting oil, and observing drilling or boring machine operation to find problems; and they use calipers and micrometers and gauges to verify dimensions and tolerances, replace and sharpen worn tools, perform equipment and tooling maintenance, and record and report anomalies. U.S. definition: the BLS 2025 wage data median is 49,080 USD per year (23.60 USD per hour), with annual percentiles of 36,300 / 41,710 / 49,080 / 57,940 / 68,410 USD (hourly percentiles 17.45 / 20.05 / 23.60 / 27.85 / 32.89); the O*NET summary page gives 2024 employment of about 5,300, a 2024—2034 projection of 'decline (Decline, -1% or lower)', and about 400 projected job openings (that source gives only the category rather than a single precise percentage, and this page follows the source wording); the preparation level is Job Zone 1-2 (SVP below 6.0), the education feedback is 57% high school or equivalent and 12% some college no degree and 12% associate degree, the interest code is RC, and there are 17 tasks; the work context includes teamwork 'extremely important' 56%, face-to-face discussions every day 52%, continuous contact with others 51%, telephone conversations every day 21% (another 44% never), email use every day 35% (another 42% never), decision freedom 'very large' 40%, precision or accuracy 'extremely important' 70%, time pressure every day 51%, work hours 'regular' 80%, standing continuously 25% + more than half 50%, continuous use of hands 57% + more than half 33%, exposure to hazardous equipment every day 54%, exposure to contaminants every day 61%, wearing common protective or safety equipment every day 93%, exposure to noise every day 56%, exposure to extreme heat or extreme cold 'weekly or more' 29%, pace determined by equipment speed 'extremely important' 52%, automation level 'moderately automated' 43%, repeating the same tasks 'extremely important' 26%, and consequences of error 'extremely serious' 29% (another 27% very serious, 26% serious). Mainland China definition: safety guards for metal cutting machine tools follow the current mandatory national standard General Technical Specifications for Safety Guards of Metal Cutting Machine Tools (GB 15760-2025, published 2025-08-01 and implemented 2026-08-01, fully replacing 8 old standards including GB 15760-2004); the occupational levels of mechanical cold working personnel are divided from level five/junior worker to level one/senior technician under national vocational skill standards (such as lathe operator 6-18-01-01, milling machine operator 6-18-01-02, grinding machine operator 6-18-01-04, and so on, Ren She Ting Fa [2018] No. 145); production and business units should implement the all-staff work safety responsibility system and the dual prevention mechanism of graded safety risk control and hidden danger investigation and treatment (Work Safety Law of the People's Republic of China, amendments effective from 2021-09-01); employers should establish and improve the occupational disease prevention responsibility system and bear responsibility for the occupational disease hazards generated by their unit and participate in work injury insurance according to law (Occupational Disease Prevention and Control Law of the People's Republic of China, fourth amendment on 2018-12-29). The above is cited by standard and regulation name and general requirements, and article numbers were not verified one by one. This occupation has no unified access-type occupational qualification in mainland China.
